prompt: What lets a database say which schema changes it has already received?
hint: The tool keeps something inside each database.

choices.text: The date of the last deploy, kept in the repository's README
choices.why: The README knows nothing about a particular database.

choices.text: A table listing the migration numbers applied to it
choices.why: Right. Reading it says where that database is.

choices.text: The size of the data directory
choices.why: Size says nothing about which changes ran.

choices.text: A comment at the top of schema.sql
choices.why: schema.sql ran once by hand and records nothing per database.

prompt: A migration added a column, and a week later it turns out to be wrong. Production has written data into it since. What is the usual way out?
hint: What would a down migration do to the data?

choices.text: Run the down migration in production
choices.why: A down that drops the column drops the week's data with it.

choices.text: Edit the old migration file and apply it again
choices.why: Databases that already applied it would never run the edit.

choices.text: A new migration that corrects it
choices.why: Right. History only moves forward, and the data is kept.

choices.text: Delete the row of that migration from the history table by hand
choices.why: Then the tool tries to apply it again over a column that exists.

prompt: Match each migration tool to how one migration is written.

pairs.right: one file with `-- +goose Up` and `-- +goose Down`

right_distractors: a Go struct read by AutoMigrate

prompt: In goose, what decides the order in which `00001_events.sql` and `00002_tickets.sql` are applied?
hint: Look at the start of each name.

choices.text: The time each file was last modified on disk
choices.why: goose reads versions from names, not from timestamps on disk.

choices.text: Alphabetical order of the table names inside
choices.why: goose never reads the SQL to order files.

choices.text: The number at the front of the name
choices.why: Right. It is the migration's version.

choices.text: The order they appear in sqlc.yaml
choices.why: sqlc.yaml names a directory, not files in order.

prompt: After `goose up` applied two migrations, `goose_db_version` held three rows. Where did the third come from?

choices.text: The INSERT of two events in the first migration
choices.why: Those rows went into events, not into goose's table.

choices.text: The status command, which records each check it makes
choices.why: status reads the table and writes nothing.

choices.text: Version 0, written the first time
choices.why: Right. Rows 1 and 2 are the two migrations.

choices.text: sqlc generate
choices.why: sqlc reads migration files; it writes Go, not rows.

prompt: `goose down` was run once after `up` had applied versions 1 and 2. What was undone?

choices.text: Both migrations, back to an empty database
choices.why: `events` was still listed by `\dt`.

choices.text: Only version 2
choices.why: Right. down undoes the last migration only.

choices.text: Nothing, because down needs a version number
choices.why: It reported `OK 00002_tickets.sql`.

choices.text: The rows of events, keeping the table
choices.why: Down runs the file's Down SQL, which dropped tickets.

prompt: Why does the lesson drop and recreate the boxoffice database before the first `goose up`, instead of just running it?
hint: What does the hand-made database lack?

choices.text: It has events and no history
choices.why: Right. In production you would mark version 1 as applied instead.

choices.text: goose refuses to connect to a database created with createdb
choices.why: It connects to any PostgreSQL database.

choices.text: The tickets table is already there
choices.why: tickets is new in this lesson.

choices.text: sqlc needs an empty database to generate
choices.why: sqlc needs the tables to exist, the opposite.

prompt: sqlc.yaml now says `schema: ___`, so the numbered files are the one place the schema is written.
What does `//go:embed migrations/*.sql` give boxoffice?

choices.text: A goose command installed beside it
choices.why: The library runs inside boxoffice; no command is needed.

choices.text: The SQL files, compiled in
choices.why: Right. No directory has to sit beside the binary.

choices.text: Migrations generated from the Go structs
choices.why: That is AutoMigrate's approach in lesson 7.

choices.text: A copy of the database
choices.why: Only the files are embedded.

prompt: Three copies of boxoffice start at the same moment against one empty database. What does the session locker do?

choices.text: One applies them while the other two wait
choices.why: Right. When the lock is free, there is nothing left to apply.

choices.text: Each copy applies the migrations in its own transaction, and two fail
choices.why: The lock is what prevents three attempts at once.

choices.text: It stops the two later copies from starting at all
choices.why: They wait, then start normally.

choices.text: It locks the events table until a restart
choices.why: The lock lasts only for the migration run.

prompt: boxoffice is started a second time against a database already at version 2. What does its log show about migrations?

choices.text: Both migrations applied again, faster
choices.why: Applied migrations are never run twice.

choices.text: An error that the tables already exist
choices.why: goose knew from its table that nothing was pending.

choices.text: A line saying the database is behind
choices.why: It was at the newest version.

choices.text: Nothing: only the listening line
choices.why: Right. There was nothing pending.

prompt: A new index on a table of a hundred million rows takes minutes to build. Why is that a problem for migrating at start-up specifically?
hint: What does the server do while migrating?

choices.text: PostgreSQL refuses migrations longer than a minute
choices.why: There is no such limit.

choices.text: go:embed cannot hold a migration that large
choices.why: The file is a few lines; the table is what is large.

choices.text: It answers no health checks meanwhile
choices.why: Right. A separate migration step keeps start-up fast.

choices.text: The advisory lock expires after a minute
choices.why: The lock lasts as long as the session holds it.

prompt: Which changes let old and new copies of boxoffice run against the same schema during a deploy? Choose all that apply.
hint: Changes both versions can live with.

choices.text: Add a column before the code uses it
choices.why: Right. Old code ignores it.

choices.text: Drop a column the old code still reads
choices.why: Old copies fail on their next query.

choices.text: Drop a column only after nothing reads it
choices.why: Right. Both versions are already past it.

choices.text: Rename a column in one migration while both versions run
choices.why: The old code still uses the old name.

prompt: In psql, the INSERT inside the transaction failed, and then COMMIT was typed. What did PostgreSQL answer?
hint: The last lines before the SELECT.

choices.text: COMMIT, keeping the UPDATE
choices.why: sold stayed at 2, so the UPDATE was not kept.

choices.text: An error asking which statement to keep
choices.why: There is no partial commit.

choices.text: WARNING and a partial commit
choices.why: Nothing partial survived: sold stayed at 2.

choices.text: ROLLBACK
choices.why: Right. A broken transaction is thrown away whole.

prompt: Why does `pgStore.Sell` write `defer tx.Rollback(ctx)` right after `Begin`, when it also calls `Commit`?

choices.text: An early return discards it
choices.why: Right. Otherwise the connection goes back to the pool mid-transaction, holding locks.

choices.text: Rollback after Commit undoes the commit, as a safety check
choices.why: After a successful Commit, Rollback does nothing.

choices.text: pgx refuses to commit without a deferred rollback
choices.why: pgx has no such rule; the defer is for the error paths.

choices.text: It makes the transaction faster
choices.why: Speed has nothing to do with it.

prompt: What does `s.q().WithTx(tx)` change about the generated `SellSeats` and `InsertTicket`?

choices.text: They are regenerated with BEGIN and COMMIT inside them
choices.why: Nothing is regenerated; only where queries are sent changes.

choices.text: They send their SQL through the transaction's connection
choices.why: Right. Same functions, routed through tx.

choices.text: They start retrying on error 40001
choices.why: WithTx adds no retries.

choices.text: They take a lock on the events table
choices.why: Locks come from the statements, not from WithTx.

prompt: Put the steps of a successful `pgStore.Sell` in order.
items: `s.pool.Begin` takes a connection and sends BEGIN
`SellSeats` takes the seats if enough are left
`InsertTicket` records the ticket and returns its id
The handler answers 201 with the ticket id

prompt: "Read, then write" recorded 27 sold for 50 sales in one run and 17 in the next. What happened to the rest?
hint: Many transactions read the same value.

choices.text: They were refused with 40001
choices.why: The refusal count was 0 at READ COMMITTED.

choices.text: Lost updates: later writes erased earlier ones
choices.why: Right. Each wrote the same number plus one.

choices.text: The goroutines that sold them crashed before committing anything at all
choices.why: No error was logged; the commits succeeded with stale numbers.

choices.text: The pool ran out of connections
choices.why: Requests waited for connections and all ran.

prompt: At REPEATABLE READ the counts added up (16 sold plus 34 refused) yet 34 buyers were told no. What must code at that level do?

choices.text: Answer those buyers with 409 Conflict
choices.why: There were seats; telling them it is sold out is false.

choices.text: Catch 40001 and run the whole transaction again
choices.why: Right. The refusal is a request to retry, not a sold-out answer.

choices.text: Lower the level to READ COMMITTED for those requests
choices.why: That brings the lost updates back.

choices.text: Retry only the UPDATE statement
choices.why: The read is stale too; the transaction is repeated whole.

prompt: Why is boxoffice's `SellSeats` exact under concurrency without FOR UPDATE or a stricter level?
hint: Look at where the check is.

choices.text: Check and change are one statement
choices.why: Right. The second buyer finds seats - sold too small.

choices.text: pgx serialises every query sent by one pool
choices.why: A pool runs several queries at once.

choices.text: Go's mutex in pgStore
choices.why: pgStore has no mutex; memStore did.

choices.text: Each request gets its own table
choices.why: All share the events table.

prompt: Match each way of selling a seat to what the race program measured.

pairs.right: 50 sold, transactions queued for the row

prompt: A transaction refused at REPEATABLE READ for a concurrent update carries SQLSTATE ___.
With MaxConns 2, six one-second queries and a 2.5 s deadline each, why did two of them fail?
hint: When did the last two get a connection?

choices.text: PostgreSQL limits pg_sleep to two at a time
choices.why: The limit was the pool's two connections.

choices.text: Their contexts were cancelled by the first two queries
choices.why: Each had its own context with its own deadline.

choices.text: They waited 2 s for a connection, leaving 0.5 s for a 1 s query
choices.why: Right. Waiting for the pool spends the query's own deadline.

choices.text: The pool gave up waiting for them
choices.why: Stat said 0 gave up waiting; they got connections and ran out of time.

prompt: max_connections is 100. Three copies of boxoffice run with MaxConns 10. How many connections can the three pools hold at most together?
Twenty buyers hit an event with five seats, and fifteen got no answer for five seconds. Which line caused it?
hint: A sold-out buyer inside a transaction.

choices.text: `SellSeats`, whose UPDATE locks the whole table
choices.why: It locks one row and finishes quickly.

choices.text: `InsertTicket`, which waits for the foreign key
choices.why: Sold-out buyers never reached the insert.

choices.text: `if _, err := s.Get(ctx, id)`, asking the pool for a second connection while holding one
choices.why: Right. Ten holders each waiting for an eleventh: nobody proceeds.

choices.text: `tx.Commit`, which blocks until all twenty finish
choices.why: Commits do not wait for other requests.

prompt: What ended the stuck requests after five seconds in that run?
hint: The rush client had a limit.

choices.text: PostgreSQL killed the idle transactions
choices.why: Nothing on the database side intervened.

choices.text: WriteTimeout closed the connections
choices.why: WriteTimeout is ten seconds and does not cancel contexts.

choices.text: The client gave up, net/http cancelled the request contexts, and the waits returned
choices.why: Right. The log shows context canceled after 5.000906 s, as 500s.

choices.text: The pool grew to 20 connections
choices.why: MaxConns stayed 10.

prompt: What rule does the fix in `Sell` follow?

choices.text: Inside a transaction, query through it
choices.why: Right. Never wait for a second resource from the pool you hold one of.

choices.text: Never call Get from a store method
choices.why: Get is fine outside a transaction.

choices.text: Raise MaxConns above the number of buyers
choices.why: A bigger pool only moves the threshold; the cycle remains.

choices.text: Commit before checking whether the event exists
choices.why: There is nothing to commit on a sold-out path.

prompt: After the fix, how many of the twenty buyers got 409?
Which file holds the transaction that writes the sale and the ticket?

choices.text: `pgstore.go`
choices.why: Right. Every query of it goes through the transaction.

choices.text: `migrate.go`, run at start
choices.why: migrate.go applies migrations.

choices.text: `events.go`, in the handler
choices.why: The handler only calls Store.Sell.

choices.text: `migrations/00002_tickets.sql`
choices.why: That file creates the table.

prompt: Why was `schema.sql` deleted in this lesson?
hint: Where is the schema written now?

choices.text: goose cannot run in a directory that contains it
choices.why: goose reads only the migrations directory.

choices.text: It had a syntax error
choices.why: It ran fine in lesson 6.

choices.text: go:embed would compile it into the binary by mistake
choices.why: The pattern is migrations/*.sql.

choices.text: It became migration 1
choices.why: Right. One place for the schema.

prompt: A colleague's handler opens a transaction and, inside it, calls a helper that runs `pool.QueryRow`. Under load the service freezes. What do you change?

choices.text: Double MaxConns
choices.why: The cycle still forms at twice the load.

choices.text: Switch the transaction to REPEATABLE READ
choices.why: Isolation does not change how connections are held.

choices.text: Hand it the tx to query through
choices.why: Right. One connection per request, no waiting on the pool while holding it.

choices.text: Add a mutex around the handler
choices.why: That serialises every request and hides the cause.

prompt: Put what happens when boxoffice starts against an empty database in order.
items: main reads the tokens and DATABASE_URL
migrate takes the advisory lock and applies 00001 and 00002
the pool is built with MaxConns 10 and pinged
the server logs that it is listening
